Title: Claude Shannon
Chunks: 4,5,6,7,42,43,44,45,47,48,49,54,55,56
His 1948 paper "A Mathematical Theory of Communication" laid the foundations for the field of information theory,[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claude_Shannon#cite_note-IEEEITS-14)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claude_Shannon#cite_note-Fortune2-19) referred to as a "blueprint for the digital era" by electrical engineer Robert G. Gallager[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claude_Shannon#cite_note-TechReview7.1.01-20) and "the Magna Carta of the Information Age" by _Scientific American_.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claude_Shannon#cite_note-21)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claude_Shannon#cite_note-22) Golomb compared Shannon's influence on the digital age to that which "the inventor of the alphabet has had on literature".[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claude_Shannon#cite_note-Fortune2-19) Shannon is also regarded as the most important post-1948 contributor to the theory. Advancements across multiple scientific disciplines utilized Shannon's theory—including the invention of the compact disc, the development of the Internet, the commercialization of mobile telephony, and the understanding of black holes.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claude_Shannon#cite_note-23)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claude_Shannon#cite_note-24) He formally introduced the term "bit",[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claude_Shannon#cite_note-QuantaMagazine-3)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claude_Shannon#cite_note-25) and was a co-inventor of both pulse-code modulation and the first wearable computer. He also invented the concept of a signal-flow graph and evaluation of the graph determinant.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claude_Shannon#cite_note-Chen1976-1-26)

Shannon joined the Central Intelligence Agency's Special Cryptologic Advisory Group in 1951. From 1956 to 1978, he was a professor at MIT. He also made numerous contributions to the field of artificial intelligence,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claude_Shannon#cite_note-PortraitsInSilicon-5) including co-organizing the 1956 Dartmouth workshop, considered to be the discipline's founding event,[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claude_Shannon#cite_note-McCarthy-27)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claude_Shannon#cite_note-Solomonoff-28) and papers on the programming of chess computers.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claude_Shannon#cite_note-CompSimBehavior-29)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claude_Shannon#cite_note-DebuggingGameHist-30) His Theseus machine was the first electrical device to learn by trial and error, being one of the first examples of artificial intelligence.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claude_Shannon#cite_note-IEEESpectrum1.25.22-8)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claude_Shannon#cite_note-MIT-31)

The Shannon family lived in Gaylord, Michigan. Claude was born in a hospital in nearby Petoskey.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claude_Shannon#cite_note-bmfrs-6) His father, Claude Sr. (1862–1934), was a businessman and, for a while, a judge of probate in Gaylord. His mother, Mabel Wolf Shannon (1880–1945), was a language teacher, who also served as the principal of Gaylord High School.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claude_Shannon#cite_note-FOOTNOTESloaneWyner1993xi-32) Claude Sr. was a descendant of New Jersey settlers, while Mabel was a child of German immigrants.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claude_Shannon#cite_note-bmfrs-6) Shannon's family was active in their Methodist Church during his youth.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claude_Shannon#cite_note-Soni_Goodman_2017_p._6-33)
Claude Shannon c.1932
Most of the first 16 years of Shannon's life were spent in Gaylord, where he attended public school, graduating from Gaylord High School in 1932. Shannon showed an inclination towards mechanical and electrical subjects. His best subjects were science and mathematics. At home, he constructed such devices as models of planes, a radio-controlled model boat and a barbed-wire telegraph system to a friend's house a half-mile away.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claude_Shannon#cite_note-34) While growing up, he also worked as a messenger for the Western Union company.
Shannon's childhood hero was Thomas Edison, who he later learned was a distant cousin: the two were descendants of John Ogden (1609–1682), a colonial leader and an ancestor of many distinguished people.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claude_Shannon#cite_note-MIT_obituary-35)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claude_Shannon#cite_note-sloane-wyner93-36)

In 1932, Shannon entered the University of Michigan, where he was introduced to the work of George Boole. He graduated in 1936 with two bachelor's degrees: one in electrical engineering and the other in mathematics._[citation needed_]
In 1936, Shannon began his graduate studies in electrical engineering at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), where he worked on Vannevar Bush's differential analyzer, which was an early analog computer that was composed of electromechanical parts and could solve differential equations.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claude_Shannon#cite_note-37) While studying the complicated _ad hoc_ circuits of this analyzer, Shannon designed switching circuits based on Boole's concepts. In 1937, he wrote his master's degree thesis, _A Symbolic Analysis of Relay and Switching Circuits,_[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claude_Shannon#cite_note-SymbolicAnalysis-38) with a paper from this thesis published in 1938.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claude_Shannon#cite_note-SymbolicAnalysis-38) A revolutionary work for switching circuit theory, in it Shannon diagramed switching circuits that could implement the essential operators of Boolean algebra. Then he proved that his switching circuits could be used to simplify the arrangement of the electromechanicalrelays that were used during that time in telephone call routing switches. Next, he expanded this concept, proving that these circuits could solve all problems that Boolean algebra could solve. In the last chapter, he presented diagrams of several circuits, including a digital 4-bit full adder.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claude_Shannon#cite_note-SymbolicAnalysis-38) His work differed significantly from the work of previous engineers such as Akira Nakashima, who still relied on the existent circuit theory of the time and took a grounded approach. Shannon's ideas were more abstract and relied on mathematics, thereby breaking new ground with his work, with his approach dominating modern-day electrical engineering.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claude_Shannon#cite_note-39)
